items: The algorithm has two loops, each iterating through the array N  times.
While there are two separate loops, they don’t affect each other in terms of scaling, so the time complexity remains O(N).
Big O Notation: O(N).
Here, we have two loops, one nested inside the other. The outer loop runs N times, and for each iteration of the outer loop, the inner loop also runs N times.
The total number of iterations is N × N, so the overall time complexity is O(N²).
Big O Notation: O(N²).
This example iterates through each element in the array and forms pairs with elements that appear later in the array, avoiding repeating pairs.
The number of iterations reduces with each step: the outer loop runs N times, and the inner loop runs N-1, N-2, etc. times.
The total number of iterations sums up to N(N-1)/2, which simplifies to O(N²).
Big O Notation: O(N²).
Here, two arrays are involved, and the algorithm has two nested loops: one iterating over arrayA and another over arrayB.
If arrayA has a elements and arrayB has b elements, the outer loop runs a times, and the inner loop runs b times.
The total number of iterations is a × b, so the time complexity is O(a × b).
Big O Notation: O(a × b).

subsections.heading: Example 5: Constant Work in Nested Loops

items: This example introduces a constant factor within the innermost loop. The outer two loops still run over arrayA and arrayB, leading to  a × b iterations.
The innermost loop runs 100,000 times for each pair, but since the constant factor doesn’t depend on the input size, it doesn’t affect the overall time complexity.
Big O Notation: O(a × b) (constant factors like 100,000 are ignored).
The algorithm iterates through only half of the array, swapping elements at each end. Since the array has N elements, the number of iterations is N/2, which simplifies to O(N).
Big O Notation: O(N).

content.text: Which of the following are equivalent to O(N)?

items: O(N + P), where P < N
O(2N)
O(N + log N)
O(N + M)
O(N + P): Since P < N, it simplifies to O(N).
O(2N): Constant factors are ignored in Big O, so this is equivalent to O(N).
O(N + log N): O(N) dominates, as log N grows slower than N.
O(N + M): There’s no relationship between N and M, so they remain separate. The time complexity is O(N + M).

content.text: Sort an array of strings, where each string is sorted individually, and then sort the array.

items: Sorting each string: O(s log s), where s is the length of the string.
Sorting a strings: O(a × s log s), where a is the number of strings.
Sorting the array of strings by comparing the strings: O(a × s log a).
The total time complexity is O(a × s (log a + log s)).

subsections.heading: Example 9: Recursive Sum of a Binary Tree

items: The function recursively visits every node in the tree. Since each node is visited once and the work done per node is constant, the time complexity is proportional to the number of nodes N.
Big O Notation: O(N).
The loop checks divisibility from 2 up to the square root of n (since if a number is divisible by any number larger than its square root, the corresponding factor will already have been found).
The number of iterations is proportional to √n, so the time complexity is O(√n).
Big O Notation: O(√n).
The function calculates the factorial of n recursively, making one recursive call for each integer down to 1.
Since there are n recursive calls, the time complexity is O(n).
Big O Notation: O(n).
This recursive function generates all permutations of a string. For a string of length n, there are n! possible permutations.
Each permutation takes  O(n) time to print. Therefore, the overall time complexity is: O(n × n!), considering the factorial number of calls and the string concatenation at each level.
Big O Notation: O(n × n!).
This recursive approach to calculating Fibonacci numbers makes two recursive calls for each call.
The number of calls grows exponentially, resulting in a time complexity of O(2ⁿ).
Big O Notation: O(2ⁿ).
The allFib function prints all Fibonacci numbers from 0 to n. For each value of i (from 0 to n-1), it calls the fib(i) function.

The fib(n) function is recursive and computes Fibonacci numbers using the classic method. This function has an exponential time complexity of  O(2ⁿ), because it makes two recursive calls for each number. However, since fib(i) is being called n times, the total amount of work isn't just  n × O(2ⁿ). Instead, it’s the sum of the work done for each Fibonacci calculation:  The total work is the sum of these values: O(1) + O(2) + O(3) + \dots + O(2^n) This sum is dominated by the largest term, O(2ⁿ), meaning the overall time complexity is O(2ⁿ).
Big O Notation: O(2ⁿ).
This version of the Fibonacci calculation uses memoization, where previously computed Fibonacci values are stored in an array (memo), so they don't need to be recalculated.
The fib(n, memo) function checks if the value has already been computed (cached) in the memo array. If not, it computes the Fibonacci number recursively and stores the result in the array.
Each Fibonacci number is calculated only once, and each call to fib(n) after that is a lookup in the array, which takes  O(1) time.
The total number of calls to fib(n) is n, and each call takes O(1) time due to the memoization, so the overall time complexity is O(n).
Big O Notation: O(n).

The powersOf2(n) function prints the powers of 2 from 1 through n by recursively dividing n by 2 until it reaches the base case (when n == 1). For each recursive call, it prints the current power of 2. Let’s break down the recursion:  The number of times n can be halved until it reaches 1 is \log₂(n), meaning the function makes O(\log n) recursive calls.
Each recursive call prints a single power of 2, and since there are O(\log n) calls, the total time complexity is  O(\log n).
Big O Notation: O(\log n).
Big O notation is a mathematical way to describe the efficiency of an algorithm, focusing on how its runtime or space requirements grow as input size increases.
It is crucial for evaluating algorithms' performance and determining which one is best suited for a particular problem.
Understanding Big O helps you:
Scenario: You need to send a file to a friend across the country.
O(1) – Constant Time Time does not depend on the size of the input. Example: Accessing an element in an array by index.
O(\log ⁡N)  – Logarithmic Time Time grows slower as the input size increases. Example: Binary search.
O(N) – Linear Time Time grows directly proportional to the input size. Example: Traversing an array.
O(N\log⁡N) – Linearithmic Time Combines linear and logarithmic growth. Example: Merge sort or heap sort.
O(N2) – Quadratic Time Time grows exponentially with input size (not efficient for large inputs). Example: Nested loops in a brute-force algorithm.
O(2^N) – Exponential Time Time doubles with each additional input. Example: Recursive algorithms solving the Tower of Hanoi.

Algorithms can depend on more than one variable.
Example: Painting a fence of width w , height h , and  p layers:. O(w⋅h⋅p)
Best Case: Minimum time an algorithm can take. Often ignored, as it is unrealistic. Example: O(N) for quicksort if all elements are equal.
Worst Case: Maximum time an algorithm can take. Most useful for evaluating reliability. Example: O(N^2) for quicksort when the pivot selection is poor.
Expected Case: Average time an algorithm takes. Example: O(N\log⁡N) for quicksort with random pivot selection.
Big O (O): Upper bound of runtime. Describes the worst-case performance. Example: Printing all elements in an array is O(N), but it could also technically be O(N^3) (though this isn't tight).
Big Omega (Ω): Lower bound of runtime. Describes the best-case performance. Example: Printing all elements in an array is Ω(N) since it can't be faster.
Big Theta (Θ): Tight bound of runtime. Describes both upper and lower bounds. Example: Printing all elements in an array is Θ(N).

content.text: Note: In industry, people use Big O to refer to the tight bound (similar to  Θ).

Constants in runtime or space complexity are irrelevant for asymptotic analysis.
Example:
Big O describes scaling, not exact performance. For a large enough input size, constant factors become insignificant.
When analyzing algorithms, we only consider the dominant term in the runtime expression.
Examples:
Some expressions cannot be simplified unless further input relationships are known.
Example:  O(A^2 + B)  remains as-is unless  A and B  are related.
If two parts of an algorithm run independently, their runtimes are added.
If one part is executed for each iteration of another, their runtimes are multiplied.

Runtime: O(\log⁡N)
Similarly, finding an element in a balanced binary search tree takes O(\log⁡ N) because the problem space is halved at every level.
When problem size reduces by a factor (e.g., halving), runtime is O(\log N).
Logarithmic bases don't matter in Big O because they differ by a constant factor.

content.text: Analyzing recursive functions often involves identifying:

items: The number of branches at each recursive call.
The depth of recursion.
Branches: Each call to f(n) makes 2 recursive calls.
Depth: The recursion continues until n = 1, so depth = n.
At depth k, there are  2^k calls.
Runtime: O(2^n).
Although there are O(2^n) calls in total, at most O(n) calls exist on the stack simultaneously (equal to the recursion depth).
Space Complexity: O(n).
